Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Aisha, a 35-year-old police officer married for eight years, had always prided herself on her strength and composure. That changed on a Tuesday evening three years ago when she responded to a domestic disturbance call in a rundown apartment building. The suspect had barricaded himself in the back bedroom, and when she entered alone to de-escalate, he overpowered her, pinning her to the floor with his weight, holding her down by her thighs and forcing himself on her. In the months that followed, the sequence of events became fractured. She could remember the dispatcher's voice, the smell of stale cigarette smoke, the way the floorboards creaked beneath her boots, but the minutes between her entry and the sound of backup arriving existed only as a black void no matter how often she tried to force them into view. When the memory returned unbidden—triggered by a sudden bang, a raised voice, or even the metallic click of her own holster—she felt a sharp, searing pain in her lower abdomen and the inside of her thighs, exactly where he had held her down. Alongside it came a rage so fierce it left her trembling and dizzy, a fury she directed at him but also at herself, for being so foolish, for not seeing it coming, for allowing herself to be cornered.

Quickly, Aisha came to believe that someone else—someone stronger, less naive, more deserving of the badge—would never have ended up on that floor. She felt that she had failed not only herself but her community, the very people she had vowed to protect, and with that failure came a profound sense of disconnection. The easy camaraderie she once shared with her fellow officers had evaporated; she no longer felt like she belonged in their world, and she assumed they could see the damage written across her face. She was certain she had permanently changed for the worse, that the confident, decisive woman her husband had married was gone, replaced by someone fragile and ashamed.

To manage the overwhelming dread that now shadowed every day, Aisha began to avoid anything that might stir strong feelings. At work, she volunteered for administrative shifts and radio dispatch, steering clear of patrol assignments that could turn volatile. She found that even a simple disagreement with her husband over weekend plans sent her heart racing and her stomach twisting, so she began nodding along to whatever he suggested, saying yes to everything and picking no fights. She learned to keep her voice flat, her opinions hidden, her emotions tightly sealed. In quiet moments, her mind wandered relentlessly to counterfactuals: if she had taken a different route to the call that night, if she had waited for her partner, if she had called for backup the moment the door closed behind her, she would be different now, her life unrecognizably better, her marriage warmer, her career intact. These thoughts brought no comfort, only a lingering sorrow that gnawed at her every evening.

The consequences accumulated slowly. Her husband, confused by her retreat from conflict and her refusal to discuss what had happened, grew distant and hurt. He stopped asking how she was because every answer was clipped and dismissive. At the precinct, her avoidance did not go unnoticed; colleagues remarked that she no longer had their backs, and the trust that once defined her squad eroded. She lost her place in the group, no longer invited to after-shift drinks or included in informal briefings. The isolation deepened until the only people she confided in were no one at all.

What finally brought Aisha to the clinic was a night shift in early spring. A car backfired in the parking lot, and she hit the ground before she knew what she was doing, her heart pounding, her thighs aching with phantom pressure, and the rage flooding back so completely that she had to lock herself in the restroom until it passed. That night she told her husband she needed help. She comes to therapy hoping to find a way back to herself, to work without fear, to feel her marriage rebuilding. But what frightens her most is the possibility that treatment will force her to confront the gaps in her memory, that she will have to lean into the very emotions she has worked so hard to avoid, and that she will discover the person she used to be is truly gone for good.
